questions.challenge_mechanism: Two series are drawn on one chart and only one of them answers the question asked. The bars are monthly net cash flow, the line is the closing balance, and the two disagree about how many bad months there were: one negative bar against five negative balances. A candidate who reads the bars reports a business with a single difficult month; a candidate who reads the line reports five months overdrawn and a peak deficit of 15 000. The figure then withholds the opening balance altogether, so the candidate has to recover it by reversing the first month rather than reading it off, and the deepest point is not the month with the worst bar but the month after it. The final part converts all of that into a lending decision with a fixed facility, so the difference between reading 8 000 and reading 15 000 is the difference between passing and failing the test the bank applies.
questions.question:
The figure is a six-month cash-flow forecast prepared by the finance officer of a small engineering firm. The bars show the net cash flow for each month in pounds: January +3 000, February +2 000, March -8 000, April +4 000, May +5 000 and June +6 000. The line shows the closing balance at the end of each month: -9 000 at the end of January, -7 000 at the end of February, -15 000 at the end of March, -11 000 at the end of April, -6 000 at the end of May and 0 at the end of June. The opening balance at the start of January is not shown.

The finance officer presents the forecast to the bank with the comment that five of the six months are cash-positive and that the business is not therefore in any difficulty. The bank lends only by granting an overdraft facility, and it will grant one of at most £10 000 on the strength of this forecast.

(a) Determine the opening balance at the start of January and the net cash flow for the six months as a whole.

(b) Explain how the closing balance can be negative at the end of five of the six months when only March shows a negative net cash flow, and state the largest amount by which the business is overdrawn during the six months and the month in which this occurs.

(c) Justify, using figures, whether the business can operate within an overdraft facility of £10 000 on this forecast, and recommend one change to the timing of the flows that would bring it within the limit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the opening balance at the start of January and the net cash flow for the six months as a whole.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the closing balance can be negative at the end of five of the six months when only March shows a negative net cash flow, and state the largest amount by which the business is overdrawn and the month in which this occurs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Justify, using figures, whether the business can operate within an overdraft facility of £10 000 on this forecast, and recommend one change to the timing of the flows that would bring it within the limit.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The closing balance at the end of January is the opening balance plus January's net cash flow, so the opening balance is -9 000 - 3 000 = -12 000 (A1). The business therefore begins the period 12 000 pounds overdrawn, a figure the forecast does not state and which can only be found by reversing the first month. The net cash flow for the six months as a whole is the sum of the six bars: 3 000 + 2 000 - 8 000 + 4 000 + 5 000 + 6 000 = +12 000 (M1)(A1). The closing balance at the end of June confirms it, since -12 000 + 12 000 = 0.

**(b)** The closing balance is a running total, and the net cash flow is a monthly figure; the sign of a bar says nothing about the sign of the line above it. January's inflow of 3 000 does not make the business cash-positive, it reduces the overdraft from 12 000 to 9 000, and the balance stays negative because the business started the year owing 12 000 more than it held (M1). A surplus month therefore only moves the balance towards zero; it cannot lift it above zero while the opening position is negative. March's single outflow of 8 000 is larger than the combined surplus of January and February, so it takes the balance from -7 000 to -15 000, and the three surpluses that follow, totalling 15 000, are only just enough to bring the balance back to zero by the end of June (A1). The business is overdrawn by at most 15 000, at the end of March, which is the month after the deficit rather than the deficit month itself (A1): the peak in the balance follows the peak in the outflow, and the two are not the same thing.

**(c)** The deepest point of the forecast is a balance of -15 000 at the end of March, so the facility required is 15 000 and a limit of 10 000 is exceeded by 5 000 at that point (M1)(A1). The business cannot operate within a 10 000 facility on this forecast, and the failure is not marginal: the facility would be exhausted before the end of March and every payment after that point until the balance recovered would be refused, which is the month in which the surpluses of April, May and June begin to arrive (A1). A single change to the timing of the flows is enough. Deferring 5 000 of the March payment into April turns March's net cash flow into -3 000 and the end-March balance into -10 000, exactly at the limit; deferring 6 000 brings the balance to -9 000 and leaves 1 000 of headroom, and either version ends the six months with a positive closing balance of 10 000 (A1). Note that the same 5 000 could equally be found by collecting 5 000 of receivables earlier, which changes the timing without changing the total. What matters is that the change is to the timing of the March outflow and not to its size, because the business does have to make the payment eventually and the forecast is otherwise cash-generative.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (A1) for the opening balance of -12 000 with the reversal of January stated; (M1) for summing the six bars; (A1) for +12 000. Accept a candidate who obtains -12 000 by working backward from the June balance through all six months provided the arithmetic is shown. Do not accept an opening balance given as a positive 12 000: the business is overdrawn from the start.

(b) (M1) for distinguishing the monthly flow from the running balance, with January's inflow identified as a reduction of the overdraft rather than a move into credit; (A1) for the explanation that the accumulated deficit of 12 000 keeps the balance negative while each surplus month only reduces it; (A1) for 15 000 at the end of March. Award the third mark for 15 000 with March identified; 8 000, the largest single outflow, scores nothing here. A candidate who says the business is profitable in five months and illiquid in five is making the distinction the part is testing and should be credited.

(c) (M1) for comparing the deepest balance with the facility limit; (A1) for the conclusion that 10 000 is insufficient, with the 5 000 shortfall stated; (A1) for the consequence, that payments would be refused from March onwards until the balance recovers; (A1) for a quantified timing change. Accept deferring at least 5 000 of the March outflow, collecting receivables earlier, or any other change that lifts the end-March balance to -10 000 or above, provided a figure is given. Do not accept 'increase the facility' as the recommended change, because the question fixes the facility at 10 000 and asks for a change to the timing. A candidate who notes that 5 000 lands exactly on the limit and that 6 000 leaves headroom has answered the part fully.
questions.explanation:
The chart is a standard cash-flow forecast and the only unusual thing about it is how far apart the two series have been made to sit. One bar is negative out of six and five balances are negative out of six, so the same figure supports two opposite descriptions of the year, and the description chosen determines the lending decision. This is not a trick in the sense of withholding information: both series are labelled and both are drawn, and the finance officer's comment about five cash-positive months is literally true. What is false is the inference, and the inference is the thing the bank is being asked to act on.

The opening balance is deliberately absent. Recovering it is a single subtraction, but it is a subtraction inside an operator, in the sense that the closing balance is defined in terms of the opening balance and the month's flow, so the unknown has to be produced before anything else can be said. Once it is recovered, the shape of the year becomes obvious: the business is overdrawn from day one, three of the six surplus months exist only to service a standing deficit, and the whole year is a recovery from 12 000 of accumulated arrears rather than a year of healthy trading. A candidate who reads the bars instead sees two strong months, one bad month and three strong months, which is a completely different narrative and is the one the finance officer is selling.

The distinction between profit and cash is the syllabus point underneath, and this forecast makes it concrete rather than notional. A month with positive net cash flow is not a month with a positive balance, and the business could be profitable in accounting terms in every one of the six months and still be unable to pay its bills in five of them. The reverse is also true and worth noting: a loss-making month with strong cash collection can leave the balance higher than the month before.

The final part is where the item becomes a decision rather than an exercise. A facility of 10 000 against a requirement of 15 000 is a refusal, and the refusal is informative because it locates the problem precisely: not profitability, not the size of the year's surplus, but the timing of one payment in March against the arrival of three surpluses in the three months after it. That is the classic working-capital judgement, and it is almost always cheaper to move a payment by a month than to borrow against it, which is why the recommendation the question asks for is a change of timing rather than a change of amount.

provenance.inspired_by: A Level Business cash-flow forecast questions, in which a chart of monthly net cash flow is supplied with a closing balance line
provenance.adaptation: The source presents a cash-flow forecast and asks the candidate to complete missing figures in a table. Here the opening balance is omitted entirely and must be recovered by reversal, the two series are drawn so that the number of negative bars and the number of negative balances differ, and the question asks the candidate to reconcile the two readings rather than to fill in cells. A facility limit that the forecast breaches is added so that the reading determines a lending decision, and the deficit is placed two months ahead of the largest surplus so that the peak of the balance and the peak of the outflow fall in different months. All six flows and all six balances are original and were chosen so that the six-month total exactly clears the opening overdraft.
provenance.resource_origin: AQA A Level Business (7132) and Pearson Edexcel A Level Business cash-flow forecast material, in which a forecast is presented as a table or chart of monthly flows with a closing balance line

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Read the bars as the measure of the trading year, observe that five of the six months show a positive net cash flow, and conclude that the business was never short of cash because the only outflow is confined to March.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The two series answer different questions and the opening balance is not on the chart at all, so it has to be recovered from a closing balance and the flow that produced it, which reveals a standing deficit of 12 000 that no month's surplus clears. The peak of the running balance also falls in a different month from the peak of the outflow, so the worst moment of the year is not visible in the bars that look worst.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The peak requirement is read as 8 000, the largest single outflow, so the business appears to sit comfortably inside a 10 000 facility and the forecast is approved, when the balance at the end of March is -15 000 and the facility is breached by 5 000 before the April and May surpluses arrive.

verification.method: The six monthly flows and the six closing balances were checked for consistency by rebuilding the balance series from the stated flows and the recovered opening balance of -12 000, which reproduces -9 000, -7 000, -15 000, -11 000, -6 000 and 0 exactly. The opening balance was recovered independently as closing January minus January's flow. The number of negative bars and the number of negative balances were counted and found to be one and five. The deferred-payment scenarios were recomputed month by month for a 5 000 and a 6 000 deferral into April, giving minimum balances of -10 000 and -9 000 and June closing balances of 10 000 and 12 000 respectively.
solution_skeleton: Read the six bars and the six closing balances from the figure.
Reverse January to recover the opening balance of -12 000.
Sum the six flows to get the six-month net cash flow of +12 000 and check it against the opening and closing balances.
Count the negative bars and the negative balances and note that they are one and five.
Locate the minimum of the balance series at -15 000 and identify the month as March.
Compare the minimum with the facility limit, quantify the shortfall, then defer 5 000 and 6 000 of the March payment into April and confirm that the minima become -10 000 and -9 000.

questions.challenge_mechanism: A share is an average, and an average over a changing mixture can move against every one of its components. Here the firm's share rises in both regions and falls overall, because the region where it is weak is the region that grew: the North doubled in importance while the South halved. The change in the weighting more than cancels the improvement in each region, and the candidate has to say so with numbers rather than describe it as a paradox. The item then refuses to let the explanation stand alone, because the firm's own volume fell from 290 units to 258 in a market of fixed total size, so the loss is not purely a mixing artefact and the managing director's complaint is half right. Saying which half is the point of the final part.
questions.question:
The figure shows a firm's sales in two regions in two consecutive years. The overall market is 1 000 units in each year, so the total market has not grown or shrunk, but the two regions have changed size. In year 1 the North market was 400 units and the firm sold 80 of them; the South market was 600 units and the firm sold 210. In year 2 the North market was 700 units and the firm sold 147; the South market was 300 units and the firm sold 111. The figure prints the firm's share of each regional market.

The managing director tells the board that the firm has lost market share in a year in which it performed better in every single region, and asks the marketing department both to explain how that can have happened and to say what the marketing plan should do about it.

(a) Calculate the firm's overall market share in each of the two years, and the percentage growth or decline of each regional market between the two years.

(b) The firm's share of the North market and its share of the South market both rise, yet its overall share falls. Explain how both statements can be true, using the figures.

(c) Evaluate the managing director's claim that the firm lost market share because it performed worse, and recommend, with supporting figures, where the marketing plan for year 3 should concentrate its effort.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the firm's overall market share in each of the two years, and the percentage growth or decline of each regional market between the two years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The firm's share of the North market and its share of the South market both rise, yet its overall share falls. Explain how both statements can be true, using the figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate the managing director's claim that the firm lost market share because it performed worse, and recommend, with supporting figures, where the marketing plan for year 3 should concentrate its effort.

questions.answer:
**(a)** In year 1 the firm sells 80 + 210 = 290 units out of a market of 1 000, so its overall share is 290 / 1 000 = 29.0 per cent. In year 2 it sells 147 + 111 = 258 units, so its overall share is 258 / 1 000 = 25.8 per cent (M1)(A1). The North market grew from 400 to 700 units, a growth of (700 - 400) / 400 = 75 per cent. The South market fell from 600 to 300 units, a decline of (600 - 300) / 600 = 50 per cent (A1).

**(b)** An overall market share is not an average of the two regional shares taken equally; it is a weighted average in which the weight of each region is the size of that region's market. In year 1 the weights are 400 and 600, so the overall share is (400 x 0.20 + 600 x 0.35) / 1 000 = (80 + 210) / 1 000 = 0.290. In year 2 the weights are 700 and 300, giving (700 x 0.21 + 300 x 0.37) / 1 000 = (147 + 111) / 1 000 = 0.258 (M1)(A1). Both regional shares did rise, from 20.0 to 21.0 per cent in the North and from 35.0 to 37.0 per cent in the South, so the firm is right about its own performance in each region (A1). But the weight moved at the same time and moved against the firm: the North, where it holds only about a fifth of the market, grew by 75 per cent and now carries 70 per cent of the overall market, while the South, where it holds more than a third, halved. The gain from performing better in each region is more than cancelled by the loss from being under-represented in the region that grew, and the two effects together leave the overall share 3.2 percentage points lower (A1).

**(c)** The claim is half right, and the half that is wrong matters. It is wrong to say the firm performed worse: its share rose in both regions, from 20.0 to 21.0 per cent and from 35.0 to 37.0 per cent, and a rising share in a market is the clearest available evidence of competitive performance (A1). But it is true that the year was a setback, and the reason is not only the change in the mix. The firm's own volume fell from 290 units to 258, a decline of 11 per cent, in a market whose total size did not change at all; the mixture effect explains why the share fell faster than the volume did, but it does not explain the fall in volume, and a firm that sells fewer units in a static market has lost ground by any commercial measure (A1). The mixture effect also understates the danger, because the region that shrank is the region where the firm is strong: if the South keeps contracting at 50 per cent a year, the firm's strongest position disappears on its own, whatever it does about its share (M1). The marketing plan should therefore concentrate on the North. At 700 units and growing at 75 per cent, the North is where the market is, and the firm holds only 21 per cent of it. Lifting the North share to the level already achieved in the South, 37 per cent, would mean selling 259 units there instead of 147, an extra 112 units, and would raise the overall share to (259 + 111) / 1 000 = 37.0 per cent, well above the 29.0 per cent of year 1 (A1). Chasing share in the South would be harder work for less: the market there is halving, so gaining share in it means winning customers in a shrinking pool while the firm's absolute volume still falls. The recommendation is a North-led plan with a target share stated as a number, and the South treated as a market to defend rather than to grow.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for summing the firm's units in each year; (A1) for 29.0 and 25.8 per cent; (A1) for +75 per cent in the North and -50 per cent in the South. Accept the shares given as 290/1 000 and 258/1 000 without conversion to percentages.

(b) (M1) for identifying the overall share as a weighted average with the regional market sizes as weights; (A1) for the two weighted calculations producing 0.290 and 0.258; (A1) for stating the two regional shares as rising, 20.0 to 21.0 and 35.0 to 37.0; (A1) for the explanation that the weight moved towards the region where the firm is weak, with the 400-to-700 and 600-to-300 change cited. A candidate who calls the result impossible, or who says one of the figures must be wrong, scores nothing: the part is testing whether the arithmetic of a changing mixture has been understood. Do not accept a purely verbal answer that does not produce the two weighted sums.

(c) (A1) for rejecting the claim that performance fell, with the two regional increases cited; (A1) for the separate observation that the firm's own volume fell from 290 to 258 in an unchanged market, which is a real loss and not a mixing effect; (M1) for the strategic risk that the strong region is the shrinking one; (A1) for a quantified recommendation. Accept any quantified target in the North, such as matching the South's 37 per cent share, or restoring the 29 per cent overall share, provided the calculation is shown. Do not accept 'increase advertising' or 'improve the product' without a figure and a region.
questions.explanation:
The arithmetic in this item is four divisions and a subtraction, and none of it is harder than a share calculation in any other question. The difficulty is that the firm's share rises in every component and falls in the total, which looks like an error until the candidate notices that the components carry different weights and that the weights have moved. The effect has a name in statistics and appears under several names in marketing, and it is worth having because it reverses conclusions in exactly this way: a firm, a school, a hospital or a sales team can improve in every group it is measured on and still deteriorate in aggregate, provided the groups have changed size.

The figures are chosen so that neither of the two easy explanations survives. The first easy explanation is that the market grew and the firm did not keep up, which is ruled out by fixing the total market at 1 000 units in both years. The second is that the whole movement is an artefact and the firm has nothing to worry about, which is ruled out by the fall in the firm's own volume from 290 units to 258 in a market of constant size. So the candidate is left with the mixture effect as the explanation of why the share fell faster than the volume, and the volume fall as a separate and more serious fact that the mixture does not explain.

The recommendation is where the item earns its marks, because the two obvious answers are both wrong. Defending the South is defending the region where the firm is strongest, which feels prudent and is not: the market there is halving, so holding share means holding a shrinking base, and the firm's strongest position dissolves on its own. Attacking the North sounds like the harder task, because the firm holds only 21 per cent there, but the market is growing at 75 per cent and the firm already holds more than a third of the neighbouring region, so the capability exists. Growing a share in a growing market also costs less per unit than growing one in a shrinking market, because part of the growth arrives with the market rather than having to be won.

There is a general lesson about which average to quote, and it is the same one that appears in the decision about whether to report a company-wide figure or a segment-by-segment one. The overall share is what the board and the investors see, so it cannot be dismissed; the regional shares are what the business can act on, so they cannot be ignored. The mistake is to treat either as the whole truth, and the managing director's error is to read the aggregate as a verdict on performance when it is really a statement about the market the firm happens to be in.

provenance.inspired_by: AP Statistics material on Simpson's paradox and on weighted averages, including the standard market-share illustration of a share rising in every segment and falling overall
provenance.adaptation: The source presents two groups whose rates move in one direction while the combined rate moves the other, and asks for the paradox to be identified. Here the setting is a firm's market share in two regions and the numbers are chosen so that the total market is constant, which removes market growth as an explanation and forces the change in composition to carry the whole effect; the firm's own volume is also made to fall, so the candidate cannot call the result a pure artefact. The final part asks for a marketing recommendation with a quantified target, which converts an exercise in statistics into a business decision, and the recommended region is the one where the firm is weakest, which the source material gives no reason to consider.
provenance.resource_origin: AP Statistics material on Simpson's paradox and on the comparison of weighted and unweighted averages across groups, including the standard treatments built on admissions and on-time-performance data

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: See the share rise in both regions and the overall share fall, treat the pair of facts as contradictory or as a data error, and conclude that the firm grew in every market it operates in and that the overall decline must be a rounding or reporting effect.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The overall share is a weighted average whose weights are the sizes of the two markets, and the weights moved at the same time as the shares did: the North, where the firm holds a fifth of the market, grew by 75 per cent while the South, where it holds a third, halved, so the gain from performing better in each region is more than cancelled by the loss from being under-represented in the region that grew.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The loss is attributed entirely to the change in market mix and the year is dismissed as a statistical artefact, when the firm's own volume fell from 290 units to 258 in a market whose total size did not change, so there is a real loss of ground underneath the mix effect as well as a compositional one.

verification.method: Each regional share was recomputed from the units and the market sizes, and the overall shares were computed both directly from the totals and as weighted averages of the regional shares, agreeing at 0.290 and 0.258. The regional growth rates were computed as +75 per cent and -50 per cent. The North target was computed as 37 per cent of 700 units, giving 259 units against an actual 147, an increase of 112 units, and the resulting overall share was confirmed as 370/1 000. The direction of the three movements was checked explicitly: both regional shares up, the overall share down.
solution_skeleton: Compute each regional share as the firm's units divided by the market size.
Add the two regional volumes and divide by the fixed market total for each year.
Recompute the overall shares as weighted averages of the regional shares using the market sizes as weights and confirm the same two values.
Compare the two regional shares year on year and the two overall shares year on year and record that the first pair rises while the second falls.
Compute the growth of each regional market and note that the larger region in year 1 is the smaller one in year 2.
Compute the volume the firm would sell in the North at the South's share, and the overall share that would result.

questions.challenge_mechanism: Both ratios improve and the firm is weaker, and the two facts are not in conflict because a ratio is a comparison and not a quantity. Subtracting the same amount from the numerator and the denominator of a ratio above one always raises it, so paying a liability out of cash raises both the current ratio and the acid test mechanically, and the working capital is unchanged at 160 000, which means the arithmetic has measured nothing at all about the firm's position. What has changed is the composition of the firm's liquid resources: cash falls from 60 000 to 20 000 and quick assets fall from 200 000 to 160 000, so the acid-test ratio rises 6.7 per cent while the assets it compares fall 20 per cent. The judgement the candidate has to reach is that the ratios are the wrong instrument for the question being asked, and that a firm whose ratios look better precisely as its buffer disappears is being described by its indicators as stronger at the moment it becomes more fragile.
questions.question:
The figure compares three measures of one firm's liquidity before and after a decision to pay £40 000 of trade payables earlier than the agreed date, using cash held in the business. Before the payment the current ratio was 2.00 and the acid-test ratio was 1.25. After the payment the current ratio was 2.33 and the acid-test ratio was 1.33. Cash held fell from £60 000 to £20 000.

The payment reduced current assets and current liabilities by the same £40 000: cash, which is a current asset, fell by £40 000, and trade payables, which are a current liability, fell by £40 000. Inventory was not affected, and neither were trade receivables. The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities, and the acid-test ratio is current assets less inventory divided by current liabilities.

The finance director tells the board that both liquidity ratios have improved and that the payment has therefore strengthened the firm's liquidity position, and proposes to repeat the practice with the remaining trade payables.

(a) Using the ratios before the payment, calculate the firm's current assets, its current liabilities and the value of its inventory before the payment.

(b) Explain why the current ratio and the acid-test ratio both rise when £40 000 is paid out of cash to reduce trade payables, given that the payment removes two thirds of the firm's cash.

(c) Evaluate the finance director's claim that the payment has strengthened the firm's liquidity position, and recommend whether the practice should be repeated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the ratios before the payment, calculate the firm's current assets, its current liabilities and the value of its inventory before the payment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the current ratio and the acid-test ratio both rise when £40 000 is paid out of cash to reduce trade payables, given that the payment removes two thirds of the firm's cash.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate the finance director's claim that the payment has strengthened the firm's liquidity position, and recommend whether the practice should be repeated.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Write current liabilities as L. Before the payment the current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities, so current assets are 2L. After the payment both fall by 40 000, giving (2L - 40) / (L - 40) = 2.333, that is 2L - 40 = 2.333L - 93.33, so 0.333L = 53.33 and L = 160, in thousands of pounds (M1)(A1). Current liabilities are therefore £160 000 and current assets are £320 000 before the payment. The acid-test ratio is 1.25, so current assets less inventory is 1.25 x 160 = £200 000, and inventory is 320 - 200 = £120 000 (A1).

**(b)** For any ratio greater than one, subtracting the same amount from the numerator and the denominator makes the ratio larger. Writing the current assets as A and the current liabilities as L, with A greater than L, the new ratio is (A - x) / (L - x) against the old A / L, and the new one is greater whenever x is positive and A exceeds L (M1). Both ratios were above one before the payment, at 2.00 and 1.25, so both rise; this is not an economic effect but an arithmetic one, and it would happen in exactly the same way if the firm had paid the payables with borrowed money or with inventory (A1). What the ratios measure is the balance between short-term assets and short-term liabilities. Paying a liability out of cash does not change that balance: working capital, the difference between the two, stays at 320 - 160 = £160 000 before and 280 - 120 = £160 000 after. The payment changes the composition of the working capital, moving £40 000 out of cash, and leaves its size untouched, which is precisely why a ratio of the two totals does not move in the direction the cash movement would suggest (A1).

**(c)** The claim confuses a measure with the thing being measured. The arithmetic of part (b) shows that the ratios rise mechanically whenever a liability is settled out of cash and the ratio is above one, and the working capital is unchanged at £160 000, so the movement in the ratios carries no information about the firm's position at all (A1). What does carry information is the composition of the liquid resources, and it has deteriorated sharply: cash falls from £60 000 to £20 000, a reduction of 67 per cent, and quick assets, the current assets less inventory that the acid-test ratio compares against current liabilities, fall from £200 000 to £160 000, a reduction of 20 per cent. So the acid-test ratio rose 6.7 per cent while the quick assets it compares fell 20 per cent, and the current ratio rose 16.7 per cent while the cash the firm holds fell 67 per cent (A1). The firm has not improved its ability to meet an unexpected payment; it has reduced it, and it has done so while the two indicators that a lender would look at moved in the opposite direction. The practice should not be repeated (A1). Paying a supplier before the agreed date costs the firm the use of the money for the period of the credit it had been granted, and nothing in the information given states a settlement discount in return, so the firm is giving up a benefit and receiving none. The recommendation is to pay on the agreed dates unless the supplier offers a discount that exceeds the cost of the funds, to hold cash at a level tied to the working-capital cycle rather than to a ratio target, and if the board wants to measure the position properly, to report the cash balance and the quick assets alongside the ratios rather than instead of them (A1).
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for setting up the equation in one unknown from the before and after current ratios; (A1) for £160 000 of current liabilities and £320 000 of current assets; (A1) for £120 000 of inventory from the acid-test ratio. Accept candidates who find the liabilities by trial as long as the resulting ratios are checked; a candidate who assumes current liabilities of 100 and reports a current ratio of 2.67 after the payment has not used the second ratio and scores nothing.

(b) (M1) for the algebraic argument that subtracting a constant from numerator and denominator of a fraction greater than one increases it, with A greater than L stated; (A1) for the observation that working capital is unchanged at £160 000 before and after; (A1) for the conclusion that the ratios measure the balance between the two totals rather than the size of the liquid resources. Do not accept 'the ratios are wrong' or 'the ratios are misleading in this case' unaccompanied by the reason: the ratios are computed correctly and behave exactly as ratios above one must.

(c) (A1) for identifying that the ratio movement is mechanical and therefore uninformative, with the unchanged working capital cited; (A1) for the quantitative deterioration, using at least two of the cash fall from £60 000 to £20 000, the quick-asset fall from £200 000 to £160 000, and the percentage comparison between the two; (A1) for the recommendation not to repeat the practice; (A1) for a reasoned basis, such as the loss of the credit period, the absence of any stated settlement discount, or the proposal to report cash alongside the ratios. A candidate who recommends repetition because the ratios improved has failed the part; a candidate who recommends repetition but identifies the loss of the credit period as a cost to be weighed earns the recommendation mark only if the position is judged to be adequately protected, which the 67 per cent fall in cash does not support.
questions.explanation:
This item is about a specific and very common analytical error: treating a movement in an indicator as evidence about the thing the indicator is supposed to measure. The current ratio and the acid-test ratio are both legitimate measures and both are computed correctly here, and both rise. The rise is not a mistake, and it is not a quirk of this firm; it follows from the arithmetic of any fraction greater than one. So the candidate cannot dismiss the movement as an error and has to explain it, which means working out what the ratios actually compare.

What they compare, in both cases, is a total of short-term assets against a total of short-term liabilities. Settling a payable out of cash reduces both totals by the same amount, so the comparison improves even though nothing has been created. The cleanest way to see that nothing has been created is the working capital, which is unchanged at £160 000: the firm's short-term funding position is exactly what it was, and only the labels on the assets have changed. That single number is worth deriving in part (b) precisely because it stops the discussion dead.

The judgement in part (c) is the part that cannot be reached by arithmetic alone, and it is the reason the item is claimed at difficulty 5. The firm has removed two thirds of its cash, and the acid-test ratio describes the firm as having moved from 1.25 to 1.33 — a 6.7 per cent improvement in a period in which the assets that ratio measures fell 20 per cent. A finance director reading only the ratio sees improvement; a supplier reading only the cash balance sees a firm that has gone from comfortably liquid to thin. Both readings are of the same accounts, and the professional task is to say which question is being asked. If the question is whether the firm's assets still exceed its liabilities, the ratios answer it and the answer is favourable. If the question is whether the firm can absorb a late customer payment or an unexpected bill, the ratios do not answer it and the cash balance does.

The general lesson is a caution about ratio analysis that is stated in every syllabus and rarely made concrete. Ratios are comparative, so they can improve while the business deteriorates, and the deterioration is invisible unless the absolute figures are quoted next to them. The proposed repetition of the practice is the dangerous part: one early payment of £40 000 leaves £20 000 of cash, and a second leaves nothing while both ratios rise again. It is worth noting that a firm can be made to look steadily stronger on these two measures all the way to insolvency, which is why lenders ask for the cash-flow forecast as well as the ratios, and why the answer to part (c) is a recommendation about what to report and not only about what to do.

provenance.inspired_by: Singapore-Cambridge A Level accounting material on liquidity ratios and on the use of ratios in lending decisions
provenance.adaptation: The source presents a set of ratios and asks the candidate to compute them and comment on whether the firm's position has improved. Here the direction of the movement is fixed in advance, the candidate has to recover the balance sheet from the two ratios before any comment is possible, and the figures are chosen so that the improvement in both ratios coincides with the destruction of two thirds of the firm's cash. The working capital is deliberately unchanged by the transaction, so the candidate can demonstrate that the ratios have measured nothing, and the recommendation the source material invites, that the practice be repeated, is the one the item is built to refuse.
provenance.resource_origin: Singapore-Cambridge H2 Principles of Accounting and H2 Management of Business material on ratio analysis, including the standard caution that a ratio may improve while the underlying position deteriorates

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Observe that the current ratio has risen from 2.00 to 2.33 and the acid-test ratio from 1.25 to 1.33, recall that higher liquidity ratios mean a stronger short-term position, and conclude that the early payment has improved the firm's liquidity.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: Subtracting a constant from the numerator and the denominator of a fraction greater than one always increases it, so the improvement is arithmetic rather than economic and the working capital is unchanged at £160 000, which means the ratios have measured the composition of the firm's short-term assets and not their size. The judgement the ratios invite disagrees with the cash balance and with the quick assets the acid-test ratio is supposed to compare.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The payment is judged beneficial and the practice is recommended for repetition, which would take the cash from £20 000 towards zero while both ratios rose again, so the firm is described as ever more liquid at the point where it can no longer meet an unexpected bill.

verification.method: Current liabilities were solved from the before and after current ratios, giving 160 in thousands, and confirmed by substituting back: 320/160 = 2.00 and 280/120 = 2.333. Inventory was solved from the acid-test ratio, 1.25 x 160 = 200, giving 320 - 200 = 120, and confirmed by substituting back: (280 - 120)/120 = 1.333. Working capital was checked as 320 - 160 = 160 before and 280 - 120 = 160 after. Quick assets were computed as 200 before and 160 after. Cash was confirmed to fall from 60 to 20, a reduction of two thirds.
solution_skeleton: Write current liabilities as an unknown, solve for it from the after-payment current ratio, and compute the current assets before the payment.
Use the acid-test ratio to obtain current assets less inventory and hence inventory.
Subtract the payment from both current assets and current liabilities and confirm both ratios reproduce the stated after values.
Compute working capital before and after and note that it is unchanged.
Compute quick assets before and after and the percentage change in each.
Compare the percentage movements in the ratios with the percentage movements in the cash and in the quick assets.
